canonical_statement: Among people with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, sustained loss of 5-7% of body weight improves glycemia, blood pressure, and lipids and may reduce the need for disease-specific medications.
Greater than 10% body-weight loss usually provides larger glycemic and metabolic benefits and may improve cardiovascular outcomes, MASLD/MASH, sleep apnea, physical comorbidity, and quality of life.
Some studies report type 2 diabetes remission maintained for 2-5 years after substantial weight loss, with better baseline beta-cell function among responders.
The chapter recommends a long-term physical activity goal of at least 150 minutes per week for weight loss and 200-300 minutes per week for weight-loss maintenance.
Very-low-calorie plans are generally used for no more than 3 months and require medical supervision because risks include electrolyte abnormalities, severe fatigue, and arrhythmias.

canonical_statement: Evidence supporting nutritional supplements for weight loss is limited by low-quality studies and high risk of bias, while higher-quality studies show little or no weight-loss benefit.
Many commercial weight-loss programs lack high-quality evidence, and some have been associated with serious harm.
Long-term cardiovascular outcomes data are lacking for naltrexone/bupropion and phentermine/topiramate.
Evidence for medical weight-loss devices in people with diabetes is limited, and some devices have been removed from the market.
The cost-effectiveness of metabolic surgery depends on assumptions about long-term effectiveness, safety, costs, and quality of life.
Long-term durability and safety data for GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy after metabolic surgery, including effects after discontinuation, remain limited.
Most large randomized trials of GLP-1-based obesity therapy excluded people with type 1 diabetes, limiting direct evidence for recommendation 8.29.
Studies of metabolic surgery in type 1 diabetes show inconsistent effects on A1C despite substantial weight loss.
